definition: Peak plate acceleration divided by g. The driving strength.
Dimensionless drive frequency.
Layer depth in sphere diameters.
The engine on main with no contact method. The baseline where it runs.
The engine processes huge numbers of events while simulated time barely advances. Also called a slow stretch.
Two spheres interpenetrate and the run aborts. Often the end of a stall.
The 2D conditions at Gamma 3.5 and 5 where the unmodified engine stalls with friction. Seven or eight, depending on the count used that night.
A sphere on the plate with another sphere pressed on it from above at an angle. Every stall examined is one.
Contact option 1. After each plate collision the sphere is placed one or two floating-point steps above the plate.
Contact option 3. Collisions slower than a small speed are made perfectly elastic.
Contact option 2. A sphere hitting the plate slower than a small speed sticks and rides the plate until the plate's acceleration falls to minus g.
Persistent contact. A long contact is held instead of being resolved as endless collisions, so regions of the layer can freeze.
The unmodified engine with the friction coefficient set to zero. Approved as a comparison model for phase diagrams only.
The referee's pass rule. Seven layer quantities are compared between engines, in units of the baseline's block standard deviation.
The referee's per-cycle energy bookkeeping, with a tolerance of one part in a hundred million of throughput.
A 3D condition from Figure 1 of the 1998 paper: Gamma 3, f* 0.44, 60,000 spheres.
A 3D condition from Figure 1 of the 1998 paper: Gamma 6, f* 0.84, 60,000 spheres.
Gamma 5, f* 0.44, 2400 spheres. The referee's headline long-contact test.
The layer of the 1998 paper: 60,000 spheres in a box 100 diameters wide, depth 5.42.
The 1998 simulation code. The baseline where this engine stalls.
Every sphere starts with an upward speed of half the plate's peak speed, so the first landing compacts the layer gently.

One loop per frequency in the paper's 3D layer: Gamma stepped up and down by 0.05, 25 cycles per step, one seed. A model with friction starts at Gamma 3.0 and goes down only until a step costs half a CPU-hour.
The same loop near onset with more cycles per step, to tell hysteresis from a ramp that is too fast.
The pattern's height variation in sphere diameters, from the layer's surface. Since Nov 17 it includes the half-box and whole-box wavelengths.
A separate session that tries to break each night's results. Its verdicts are holds, doubtful or broken.

Option four as built Nov 18. A chattering contact (a slow hit on the plate, a side wall, or a sphere that is already held) has its normal relative velocity kept at zero by small pushes every 5e-4 time units; sliding along the contact stays free. It lets go when keeping it would need a pull, or when something hits it faster than 0.01.
The held-contact variant where a sphere held on another moves over its surface: the contact direction is updated every step.
The held-contact variant where the contact direction stays at its value at capture: the upper sphere moves on that tangent plane and is let go once it is 1e-4 diameters off the lower sphere.
Where a friction-model loop turns on the way down: the first step whose 25 cycles cannot finish in half a CPU-hour (paper's box).
Since Nov 18: on the way up a step may use 2 CPU-hours (paper's box) before the loop stops; it only catches a true stall.
Where every nudge loop stopped on the way up on Nov 18 (Gamma 4.35 to 4.45, all frequencies): its cost per cycle rose 3 to 10 times between 4.3 and 4.45.

Option four as built Nov 18 and named by Chris on Nov 19. A chattering contact (a slow hit on the plate, a side wall, or a sphere that is already held) has its normal relative velocity kept at zero by small pushes every 5e-4 time units, solved together for each cluster of held spheres; between pushes the spheres move freely. It lets go when keeping it would need a pull, or when something hits it faster than 0.01.

A separate hybrid hard-sphere and soft-sphere code (repository grapenuts, commit 486d8eb named by Chris): lasting contacts become springs applied as small kicks between free flights. Evaluated on line L0020.
